This enrichment is biologically notable because carbohydrate-dependent recognition operates at the interface of cell surfaces and the extracellular environment, where it influences several processes that are highly relevant to depression, including immune recognition, receptor activation, cell adhesion, intercellular communication, trafficking, synapse formation, glial responses, barrier signaling, and gut-brain communication. In the context of depression, the identification of 11 proteins in this functionally coherent category supports a mechanistic framework in which glycan-sensitive proteins may connect neuroinflammation, stress-related signaling disruption, synaptic dysfunction, and peripheral-to-central immune communication, thereby extending the interpretation of depression beyond neurotransmitter-centered models toward a broader systems-level pathology.

To further contextualize these 11 proteins, the figure below illustrates their protein-protein interaction network, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/df893cca-0300-49b9-b8df-d347c044deb1.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=565C1ED811DA8975)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We introduce them in detail below, moving from proteins with more direct immune-inflammatory relevance to those whose connections to depression may be more indirect or context-dependent.

CLEC4D is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to depression because it sits at the intersection of innate immune sensing, inflammatory signal amplification, and adaptive immune polarization. Binding of microbial ligands such as mycobacterial trehalose 6,6'-dimycolate and *Candida albicans* alpha-mannans activates FCER1G-dependent immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif signaling, leading to spleen associated tyrosine kinase, caspase recruitment domain family member 9, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and subsequent promotion of T helper 1 and T helper 17 oriented immune responses. This is highly relevant to depression because a substantial body of evidence links depressive symptomatology to chronic low-grade inflammation, exaggerated innate immune activation, and increased cytokine pathways that can alter monoamine metabolism, glutamatergic signaling, neuroendocrine function, and neuroplasticity. In particular, T helper 17 associated inflammation has been increasingly implicated in stress-related neuroinflammation and blood-brain barrier dysregulation. Therefore, CLEC4D appears to be a plausible upstream contributor to inflammatory states that may increase vulnerability to depression, especially in contexts involving infection, dysbiosis, or persistent immune activation. Its endocytic and antigen-presentation roles further support a broader function in sustaining immune responses that could influence depression-related immune phenotypes.[[103]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [[104]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23911656) [[105]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971047) 

In contrast to CLEC4D, which may amplify inflammatory signaling, LGALS1 appears more consistent with an immunoregulatory role that could potentially counter excessive inflammation.

LGALS1 (galectin-1) is particularly relevant to depression because it is an immunoregulatory lectin with potent effects on T-cell fate and inflammatory balance. Its ability to induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T helper 17 differentiation suggests a role in limiting excessive inflammatory responses. This is important in depression, where immune dysregulation is often characterized not only by elevated inflammatory mediators but also by altered T-cell profiles and disturbed immune homeostasis. By restraining T helper 17 associated pathways, LGALS1 may counter mechanisms linked to neuroinflammation, microglial activation, and cytokine-driven changes in neurotransmission. In addition, its broader roles in apoptosis and cellular differentiation suggest potential relevance to tissue remodeling and stress responses beyond the immune compartment. Thus, LGALS1 stands out as a candidate modulator that could influence depression risk or severity through anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory mechanisms, especially in inflammatory subtypes of depression.[[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Shifting from immune regulation toward vascular and degenerative biology, COLEC12 may be relevant in a somewhat different but still biologically plausible manner.

COLEC12 is notable because it links innate immunity, vascular biology, and potentially neurodegenerative processes, all of which have plausible relevance to depression. Its role in recognizing pathogens and promoting phagocytosis places it within inflammatory host-defense pathways that can contribute to peripheral immune activation. More importantly, its capacity to internalize oxidatively modified low-density lipoprotein suggests involvement in oxidative stress and vascular inflammation, both of which are strongly associated with depression, particularly late-life depression and depression comorbid with cardiometabolic disease. The additional suggestion that COLEC12 may contribute to amyloid-beta clearance further increases its relevance, since depression is epidemiologically and mechanistically linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Taken together, COLEC12 may be relevant to depression through inflammatory, vascular, and neurodegeneration-associated mechanisms rather than through a direct neurotransmitter-related pathway.

A related but distinct immune context is represented by SIGLEC1, which may be more informative for antiviral and interferon-associated inflammatory states.

SIGLEC1 is relevant to depression primarily because it reflects activated myeloid and dendritic-cell states associated with antiviral immune responses. Infection and sustained immune activation are recognized contributors to depressive symptoms, and interferon-related or virus-associated inflammatory programs are especially well known to induce behavioral changes resembling depression. By facilitating viral capture and entry into activated dendritic cells, SIGLEC1 may participate in immune processes that sustain antigen presentation and inflammatory signaling. Although the function listed here is not specific to the central nervous system, it is mechanistically compatible with the broader infection-inflammation-depression framework, in which peripheral antiviral responses alter cytokine production and thereby influence brain function, mood regulation, and sickness behavior. Accordingly, SIGLEC1 may be indirectly informative for depression biology, particularly in infection-associated or interferon-driven depressive states.

Moving further from direct immune sensing, AMBP may connect carbohydrate-binding enrichment to thromboinflammatory and vascular processes that have also been implicated in some forms of depression.

AMBP may have a meaningful, albeit more indirect, connection to depression through coagulation-inflammation crosstalk. Depression has been associated in some studies with platelet activation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered coagulation profiles, especially in individuals with cardiovascular comorbidity. By inhibiting factor ten a dependent prothrombin activation, AMBP may influence thromboinflammatory pathways that intersect with systemic inflammation and vascular risk. Its inhibition of mast cell proteases is also noteworthy, because mast cells can amplify neuroimmune and stress-related inflammatory responses and have been proposed to contribute to blood-brain barrier dysfunction and neuroinflammation. Therefore, while AMBP is not a classic depression gene, its protease-inhibitory functions could be relevant in inflammatory or vascular subtypes of depression.

The next protein, MRC1, is of interest for a different reason, as the annotation provided points toward chromatin and neuronal structural regulation rather than the more typical immune interpretation.

MRC1 is highly interesting from a neurobiological perspective because the function provided here points to a chromatin-remodeling factor involved in neural development, progenitor-state transitions, and dendritic growth. Processes of chromatin remodeling and activity-dependent transcription are central to synaptic plasticity, stress adaptation, and neuronal structural remodeling, all of which are strongly implicated in depression. Reduced dendritic complexity and impaired neuroplasticity are recurring findings in depressive disorders, particularly in corticolimbic regions. Therefore, a protein involved in neuron-specific chromatin remodeling and dendrite-associated gene regulation may be relevant to depression through mechanisms affecting neuronal maturation, connectivity, and long-term transcriptional responses to stress. This makes MRC1 a potentially important candidate for understanding how epigenetic and developmental programs intersect with vulnerability to mood disorders. However, the annotation provided appears atypical for the canonical mannose receptor gene symbol MRC1, so interpretive caution is warranted.

Finally, LGALS4 appears to have the most indirect connection in this set, with its potential relevance emerging mainly through barrier integrity and tissue organization.

LGALS4 has a less direct connection to depression than CLEC4D or LGALS1, but it may still be relevant through barrier and cell-adhesion biology. Adherens junction organization is important for epithelial integrity, and disturbances in gut barrier function have been increasingly linked to depression via the gut-immune-brain axis. If LGALS4 contributes to maintaining tissue architecture and barrier-associated interactions, altered function could theoretically influence inflammatory tone, microbial translocation, and downstream neuroimmune signaling. Nevertheless, based on the functional information provided, the evidence connecting LGALS4 to depression is more speculative and indirect than for proteins with explicit immune-regulatory or neurodevelopmental roles.

### Colon; goblet cells[≥Medium] (HPA:0130892) 

The pathway described as colon goblet cells refers to the differentiation, maintenance, and functional activity of specialized secretory epithelial cells in the colonic mucosa that synthesize and release mucins and other protective factors to form the intestinal mucus barrier. In the colon, goblet cells are central to the first line of host defense because they generate the mucus layer that spatially separates luminal microorganisms from the epithelial surface, limits penetration of microbial products, supports epithelial repair, and helps preserve immune and metabolic homeostasis. Adequate goblet cell abundance and secretion are therefore essential for barrier integrity, regulation of intestinal permeability, and control of mucosal inflammation. Experimental studies further indicate that goblet cell status is tightly linked to microbial ecology, short chain fatty acid production, tight junction expression, oxidative balance, and enteric neuroimmune signaling. Because the colon is a major interface of the microbiota gut brain axis, disruption of goblet cells may promote barrier failure, inflammatory cytokine production, altered tryptophan metabolism, and abnormal neurotransmitter signaling, all of which are biologically relevant to depressive pathology. Conversely, restoration of goblet cell number or mucus production has repeatedly been associated with improved colonic homeostasis and better behavioral outcomes in stress related and inflammation related models of depression. 

Against this biological background, the literature provided here suggests a fairly consistent connection between the colon goblet cell pathway and depression through impairment of the intestinal mucus barrier and subsequent dysregulation of the microbiota gut brain axis. Multiple depression related animal models indicate that stress associated or sleep deprivation associated depressive phenotypes are accompanied by a reduction in colonic goblet cells, implying weakened mucus protection and barrier injury. Chronic sleep deprivation in female mice induced anxiety and depressive like behaviors together with decreased goblet cells, epithelial abnormalities, glandular atrophy, microbial dysbiosis, and fecal metabolic disturbances related to oxidative stress and inflammation, thereby linking goblet cell loss to mood related pathology in the setting of barrier disruption [[106]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39767560). Similarly, chronic unpredictable mild stress reduced goblet cells and crypt architecture in the colon, whereas behavioral improvement after hesperidin treatment occurred together with restoration of goblet cells, reduced inflammation, and microbiota remodeling, supporting a functional association between goblet cell preservation and antidepressant like effects [[107]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39136837). In female mice exposed to chronic restraint stress, prebiotic administration restored the stress induced decrease in colon goblet cells in parallel with improvement of anxiety related behavior and normalization of gut and blood brain barrier markers, suggesting that goblet cell dependent mucosal resilience may contribute to stress vulnerability, particularly in females [[108]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36650644). 

This pattern is further strengthened by intervention studies that more directly connect goblet cell recovery with improvement in depression related phenotypes. In treatment resistant depression models, synbiotic treatment with Faecalibacterium prausnitzii plus fructo oligosaccharides and galacto oligosaccharides increased mucus producing goblet cells while simultaneously reducing neuroinflammation, normalizing monoamine and gamma aminobutyric acid signaling, and reversing depression like behavior [[109]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39214274). Likewise, short chain fatty acid supplementation rescued anxiety and depression like phenotypes induced by stress or fecal microbiota transfer and increased mucus producing goblet cells together with restoration of short chain fatty acid receptor signaling, reduced inflammatory cytokines, and correction of kynurenine pathway abnormalities, indicating that goblet cell recovery may be part of a broader therapeutic restoration of gut barrier and brain function [[110]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38382546). Additional studies support this same general framework. Coprococcus eutactus treatment in adolescent stress exposed mice recovered goblet cells and mucus secretion while shifting tryptophan metabolism away from neurotoxic kynurenine products and improving depressive behavior [[111]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38649105), and fecal microbiota transplantation in post stroke depression increased goblet cells while improving depressive like behavior and neuroinflammation [[112]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40189067). Although some studies concern depression secondary to colitis or neurological disease rather than primary major depression, they still converge on a similar mechanism, showing that therapies which increase goblet cells also reduce colonic and cerebral inflammation, improve tight junction integrity, normalize hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis or brain derived neurotrophic factor related signaling, and alleviate depression like behavior [[113]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40188913) [[114]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39647733) [[115]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41977455) [[116]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40145348). Taken together, these findings support the interpretation that colon goblet cells may be more than histological markers of intestinal health and could participate actively in depression relevant biology by maintaining the mucus barrier, restraining inflammation, shaping microbial metabolites, and stabilizing gut to brain communication.[[106]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39767560) [[107]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39136837) [[108]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36650644) [[109]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39214274) [[110]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38382546) [[111]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38649105) [[112]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40189067) [[113]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40188913) [[114]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39647733) [[115]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41977455) [[116]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40145348) 

Consistent with the literature based observations above, the enrichment analysis also points to a quantitatively substantial convergence on this pathway. There were 23 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as colon goblet cells, a biological program centered on the differentiation, maintenance, and secretory activity of specialized epithelial cells that sustain the colonic mucus barrier, regulate intestinal permeability, constrain mucosal inflammation, and influence microbiota gut brain axis signaling processes that are highly relevant to depressive pathology. Enrichment across 23 proteins suggests a meaningful concentration of depression associated molecular signals in intestinal barrier biology and supports the possibility that mucus layer integrity, microbial separation from the epithelium, cytokine control, oxidative balance, tryptophan metabolism, and neurotransmitter related signaling may collectively contribute to depression associated molecular dysfunction in this dataset. The figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 23 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/4eb2273b-7d08-4956-b027-6ca9e7e812ad.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=C556A7268DF93348)

With this network context in place, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins in greater detail and considers their possible relevance to depression in a cautious and evidence guided manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

YAP1 is particularly noteworthy in the context of depression because its reported activation of the ERBB4 C-terminal fragment links it to neuregulin and ERBB family signaling, a pathway with established relevance to synaptic plasticity, interneuron function, and higher order affective regulation. ERBB4 signaling has been repeatedly implicated in neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric processes, and perturbation of these pathways may influence cortical circuit stability and stress responsiveness. Although the functional statement provided here is concise, the YAP1 and ERBB4 connection appears biologically meaningful because depression is increasingly understood as a disorder of maladaptive neuroplasticity rather than solely monoamine imbalance. A protein that modulates ERBB4 activity may therefore contribute to altered neuronal signaling, resilience, and mood related circuit remodeling. For this reason, YAP1 stands out as one of the more directly neuropsychiatrically relevant proteins in the present list, even though no PubMed citation was supplied in the source annotation.  

A related but distinct line of reasoning points toward inflammatory and cellular stress pathways. LGALS3, galectin 3, is among the strongest candidates for relevance to depression because it integrates inflammation, cellular stress responses, and autophagy related membrane damage sensing. Contemporary models of depression emphasize the contribution of chronic low grade inflammation, altered innate immune signaling, and dysregulated neuroimmune crosstalk. A protein that promotes monocyte and macrophage chemoattraction, mast cell activation, and neutrophil associated inflammatory programs could plausibly contribute to systemic and central inflammatory states associated with depressive symptomatology. Its additional role in pre messenger ribonucleic acid splicing suggests a broader capacity to influence stress responsive gene expression, while its cooperation with TRIM16, ATG16L1, and BECN1 connects it to autophagic quality control pathways that are increasingly implicated in neuronal homeostasis and resilience under stress. Thus, LGALS3 appears important because it lies at the intersection of inflammation, intracellular damage responses, and transcriptional and post transcriptional regulation, all of which are mechanistically relevant to depression pathophysiology.  

Extending this theme, TSPAN8 may also be relevant because it converges on several biological systems now recognized as important in mood disorders, including inflammatory cytokine processing, mechanistic target of rapamycin and protein kinase B signaling, apoptosis and autophagy balance, and intestinal barrier integrity. Its role in promoting ADAM17 mediated tumor necrosis factor alpha processing is notable because tumor necrosis factor alpha is one of the most consistently studied inflammatory mediators in depression. In parallel, the interaction with RICTOR and mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 is significant because mechanistic target of rapamycin pathway dysfunction has been linked to impaired synaptic plasticity and to antidepressant mechanisms, particularly rapid acting antidepressant responses. The reported effect on apoptosis and autophagy further strengthens its relevance, as stress related neuronal vulnerability often involves maladaptive cell survival signaling. Finally, its role in intestinal epithelial barrier maintenance and regulation of intestinal inflammation raises the possibility of gut brain axis involvement, an area of growing interest in depression research. Collectively, TSPAN8 stands out as a multifunctional regulator connecting immune, metabolic, and signaling pathways with plausible mechanistic links to depressive illness.  

Shifting from inflammatory signaling to cellular energetics, CHCHD10 is of interest for depression because mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurrent theme in the biology of stress related and mood disorders. The maintenance of mitochondrial organization and cristae architecture is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, adenosine triphosphate production, calcium buffering, and apoptotic signaling. In neurons, which are highly energy dependent, even subtle disruption of mitochondrial ultrastructure can impair synaptic transmission and plasticity, thereby affecting neural circuits involved in mood regulation. Depression has been associated with altered bioenergetics, oxidative stress, and reduced cellular resilience. Therefore, a protein implicated in preserving mitochondrial integrity may be mechanistically relevant to disease susceptibility or progression. Although the annotation is brief and lacks direct citations, CHCHD10 stands out because mitochondrial homeostasis provides a compelling bridge between cellular stress biology and depressive phenotypes.  

In comparison with the proteins above, AGR3 appears to have a more indirect and tentative connection to depression. AGR3 is not a classic depression gene, but it may still be of interest because calcium regulation is a core biological process in excitability, secretion, and stress signaling. The function provided here is centered on airway epithelial physiology rather than neural tissue. However, the mention of intracellular calcium regulation is notable given the broader importance of calcium dynamics in neuronal communication and plasticity. In depression research, dysregulated calcium signaling has been linked to altered synaptic function and stress reactivity. Nevertheless, because the annotated role of AGR3 is primarily peripheral and respiratory, its connection to depression is likely weaker and more speculative than for proteins directly involved in inflammation, mitochondrial function, or canonical neuropsychiatric signaling pathways.  

Another protein with somewhat broader neurobiological relevance is BSG, which stands out because its functions map onto several processes potentially relevant to depression, including axon integrity, myelin maintenance, neuronal survival, and neurite remodeling. Disturbances in white matter organization, connectivity, and structural plasticity have been reported in depressive disorders, and proteins involved in preserving myelinated axons may therefore have pathophysiological significance. The anti apoptotic effect on neurons and the regulation of neurite outgrowth are also relevant, since depression has been linked to reduced neuroplasticity and stress induced neuronal atrophy. At the same time, the inhibitory effect on neurite extension suggests a complex role in shaping connectivity rather than simply promoting regeneration. Overall, BSG appears important because it participates in neuron glia interactions and structural maintenance of neural circuits, processes that may influence vulnerability to mood dysregulation.[[117]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [[118]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [[119]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [[120]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [[121]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [[122]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [[123]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [[124]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [[125]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [[126]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [[127]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [[128]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [[129]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868)  

Moving from structural neural maintenance to vascular and trophic signaling, COL18A1 is potentially relevant to depression through vascular and neurotrophic mechanisms. Its anti angiogenic activity, particularly its inhibition of VEGFA signaling, is important because vascular endothelial growth factor has been implicated in neurogenesis, stress adaptation, and antidepressant responses. Although most annotations here concern endothelial biology, vascular endothelial growth factor related pathways are not confined to the vasculature and have recognized roles in the brain, including support of neurovascular coupling and hippocampal plasticity. Therefore, a factor that antagonizes VEGFA signaling could theoretically influence neurobiological resilience, tissue repair, or the neurovascular components of depressive pathology. This makes COL18A1 an interesting candidate, especially in frameworks that conceptualize depression as involving impaired plasticity and altered neurovascular support.[[38]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [[39]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123)  

A somewhat related stress biology perspective is provided by RNASE1, which may be relevant to depression because it is explicitly involved in stress responsive intracellular regulation and redox homeostasis. Oxidative stress and impaired cellular stress adaptation are well established features in many patients with depression. The ability of this inhibitor to regulate angiogenin differently under basal versus stress conditions suggests a finely tuned mechanism linking stress exposure to ribonucleic acid metabolism, cytoprotection, and possibly translational control. Its putative role in redox homeostasis further strengthens the connection, as redox imbalance can impair neuronal function and plasticity. While the depression link is indirect, RNASE1 remains biologically compelling because it participates in molecular stress adaptation pathways that may shape vulnerability or resilience in mood disorders.[[130]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [[131]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [[132]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [[133]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [[134]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [[135]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [[136]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [[137]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [[138]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170)  

From there, the remaining proteins appear to have more contextual or peripheral links to depression. CXADR has a more speculative but still potentially meaningful connection to depression because infection and immune activation are increasingly recognized as contributors to depressive symptoms in a subset of patients. A host receptor that mediates viral entry may be relevant in the context of infection triggered inflammation, sickness behavior, or post infectious neuropsychiatric sequelae. However, based on the function provided, the link to depression is indirect and substantially weaker than that of proteins involved in inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial maintenance, or neuroplasticity. Thus, CXADR is best regarded as a peripheral or contextual candidate rather than a central mechanistic driver.  

Finally, PIGR may be relevant to depression through mucosal immunity and the gut brain axis, which returns conceptually to the barrier centered theme of this pathway. Secretory immunoglobulin A is a central component of barrier immunity at mucosal surfaces, and disturbances in mucosal immune regulation have been proposed to influence systemic inflammation and microbiome host interactions, both of which may affect mood and behavior. Although the function provided is immunological rather than neural, depression is increasingly viewed as a multisystem disorder in which peripheral immune and barrier processes can shape central nervous system outcomes. PIGR is therefore of moderate interest as a marker of mucosal immune homeostasis, though its mechanistic connection to depression is less direct than that of inflammatory signaling or neuronal plasticity regulators.

### Colon; endocrine cells[High] (HPA:0131293) 

The pathway described as colon endocrine cells with high activity refers to the specialized hormone-producing epithelial cell populations distributed throughout the colonic mucosa, including enterochromaffin cells, peptide YY-producing cells, glucagon-like peptide 1-producing cells, and other neuroendocrine cell types that sense luminal nutrients, microbial metabolites, inflammatory signals, and neural inputs. These cells act as a major interface between the intestinal microbiota, the epithelial barrier, the enteric nervous system, immune cells, and distant brain regions. By releasing serotonin, neuropeptide Y-related signals, peptide YY, glucagon-like peptide 1, and other bioactive mediators, colonic endocrine cells regulate motility, secretion, appetite, mucosal permeability, immune tone, and gut-to-brain communication. Their function is tightly shaped by microbial products such as short-chain fatty acids and amino acid metabolites, as well as by stress hormones and inflammatory cytokines. Because depression is increasingly understood as a systemic disorder involving neuroinflammation, altered neurotransmission, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, barrier dysfunction, and gut microbiota imbalance, colon endocrine cells are biologically well positioned to participate in disease mechanisms. Alterations in their number, secretory activity, and signaling partners can therefore translate intestinal environmental changes into central nervous system effects relevant to mood, cognition, and stress responsivity.

Against this biological background, the collected literature supports a cautious model in which colon endocrine cells may contribute to depression through the gut-brain axis by integrating microbial, inflammatory, barrier, and neurochemical signals. The most direct evidence comes from a chronic unpredictable mild stress study showing that stress impaired colonic endocrine cell function and reduced neuropeptide Y expression in both the colon and the medial prefrontal cortex, while rifaximin restored colonic endocrine function, increased neuropeptide Y in the colon and brain, normalized neurotransmitter imbalance, and improved anxiety-like and depression-like behaviors; importantly, knockdown of neuropeptide Y in the medial prefrontal cortex abolished the behavioral benefit, indicating bidirectional colon-to-brain signaling centered on endocrine regulation in the colon [[139]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41430083). A complementary obesity-related depression study further showed that gut microbial remodeling, particularly enrichment of Anaerotruncus colihominis and glutamate production, damaged colonic barrier integrity and altered intercellular communication between colon epithelial compartments and hippocampal neurons, thereby worsening depression-like behavior, which places colonic sensory and secretory epithelial programs upstream of central mood changes [[140]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40274437). Broader mechanistic support comes from work showing that psychological stress can drive excessive serotonin release from enterochromaffin cells, disrupt epithelial barrier function, and amplify immune activation, all of which are recognized contributors to depressive pathophysiology [[141]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36806451). Human mucosal studies in irritable bowel syndrome further demonstrate that increased enterochromaffin cell number and increased tryptophan hydroxylase one expression in the caecum and descending colon correlate positively with Hamilton depression scores, linking altered colonic endocrine signaling to depressive symptom burden [[142]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34773967), while earlier histological work identified increased serotonin-containing enterochromaffin cells in postinfective irritable bowel syndrome, a condition frequently associated with mood symptoms and altered gut-brain signaling [[143]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12873581). In parallel, studies of microbial and nutritional modulation indicate that colonic endocrine output is responsive to luminal metabolites, since short-chain fatty acids stimulate secretion of glucagon-like peptide 1 and peptide YY from the colon, demonstrating a mechanism by which microbiota-derived metabolites can alter endocrine signaling with systemic metabolic and neural consequences [[144]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29494208). Finally, several intervention studies in colitis, obesity, and metabolic stress models show that treatments improving colonic inflammation, barrier integrity, microbiota composition, and gut-derived signaling simultaneously alleviate depression-like behavior, reinforcing the concept that dysfunction of colon endocrine and adjacent epithelial programs is not merely associated with depression but may participate causally in its development and maintenance [[113]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40188913) [[145]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39599597). Taken together, this pathway appears related to depression because colon endocrine cells constitute a high-activity transducer system that may convert dysbiosis, stress, and inflammation into altered neuropeptide, serotonin, and metabolic signaling, thereby influencing brain neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, and mood-related behavior.[[139]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41430083) [[140]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40274437) [[141]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36806451) [[142]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34773967) [[143]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12873581) [[144]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29494208) [[113]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40188913) [[145]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39599597) 

Building on this literature-based rationale, the enrichment result provides a quantitative basis for prioritizing this pathway in the present analysis. There were 17 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing colon endocrine cells with high activity. This pathway captures a biologically important epithelial signaling compartment in the colonic mucosa, where hormone-producing cell populations integrate nutrient-derived signals, microbial metabolites, inflammatory cues, and neural inputs to regulate secretion, motility, mucosal permeability, immune activity, and communication with distant brain regions. In the context of depression, the enrichment of 17 proteins supports the relevance of this pathway because colon endocrine cells sit at the intersection of several disease-related processes, including altered serotonin-related signaling, disturbed gut-to-brain communication, barrier dysfunction, immune activation, and stress-responsive neuroendocrine regulation. Given that the analyzed set contains 17 proteins assigned to this functionally coherent pathway, the enrichment result quantitatively indicates that a substantial disease-linked molecular subset converges on intestinal endocrine signaling mechanisms that may translate peripheral intestinal changes into central nervous system effects relevant to mood, cognition, and stress responsivity. We will introduce these proteins in detail in the following.

To facilitate interpretation of this enriched set, the figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 17 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/60da1f7f-9921-4c3f-a501-e1231a99fadf.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=E2874D80440FB0B3)

Following this network-level overview, we next describe several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the listed proteins, BSG stands out as one of the most compelling candidates for relevance to depression because its annotated functions converge on several neurobiological processes repeatedly implicated in depressive disorders: myelin maintenance, axonal integrity, neuronal survival, and structural plasticity. Major depression has increasingly been associated with white matter abnormalities, impaired oligodendrocyte function, reduced connectivity, and altered neuronal remodeling. In this context, BSG is notable because it supports maintenance of myelinated axons rather than developmental myelination per se, suggesting a role in preserving mature neural circuit integrity. Its ability to protect neurons against apoptosis further strengthens its potential relevance, since stress-related neuronal vulnerability and reduced neurotrophic support are central themes in depression pathophysiology. In parallel, BSG negatively regulates neurite outgrowth through interactions with RTN4R and RTN4RL2 and gangliosides, linking it to mechanisms of axonal remodeling and synaptic reorganization. Such functions may be particularly important in depression, where impaired structural plasticity and maladaptive circuit stabilization are thought to contribute to persistent symptoms. Overall, BSG is mechanistically connected to neurodegeneration-like features, myelin abnormalities, and reduced plasticity, all of which are highly pertinent to depression biology.[[117]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [[118]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [[119]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [[120]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [[121]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [[122]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [[123]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [[124]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [[125]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [[126]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [[127]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [[128]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [[129]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

In a complementary manner, LGALS3 appears relevant because it lies at the intersection of inflammation, innate immune activation, cellular stress responses, and autophagy, pathways that are increasingly recognized as core components of depressive pathogenesis in at least a substantial subset of patients. Neuroinflammation and altered peripheral immune signaling are among the most reproducible biological findings in depression, and LGALS3 directly participates in leukocyte activation, monocyte and macrophage recruitment, and mast cell responses, all of which could amplify inflammatory signaling capable of influencing brain function. Its role in opsonization of apoptotic cells also suggests involvement in resolution of inflammation and tissue homeostasis, processes that may be dysregulated in chronic stress states. In addition, the reported role of LGALS3 in membrane damage sensing and recruitment of ATG16L1 and BECN1 connects it to autophagy, a process linked to neuronal resilience, synaptic maintenance, and stress adaptation. The nuclear splicing function of LGALS3 further broadens its relevance, as altered ribonucleic acid processing has been implicated in psychiatric disease. Thus, LGALS3 stands out as a multifunctional protein with plausible links to immune-inflammatory and stress-response mechanisms that may contribute to depression.

Consistent with this emphasis on inflammatory and adaptive signaling, TSPAN8 is notable because its annotated activities map onto several depression-relevant systems: inflammatory cytokine signaling, mechanistic target of rapamycin and protein kinase B pathway regulation, apoptosis and autophagy balance, and gut barrier biology. The capacity of TSPAN8 to promote ADAM17-mediated tumor necrosis factor alpha processing is particularly interesting, given the extensive evidence linking elevated tumor necrosis factor alpha and inflammatory signaling to depressive symptoms and treatment resistance. Its interaction with RICTOR and mechanistic target of rapamycin complex two, leading to protein kinase B one phosphorylation, is also important because mechanistic target of rapamycin signaling is strongly implicated in synaptic plasticity and antidepressant responses, especially in the context of rapid-acting antidepressant mechanisms. Furthermore, TSPAN8 influences apoptosis and autophagy, both of which are relevant to neuronal survival under chronic stress. Finally, its role in maintaining the intestinal epithelial barrier and limiting intestinal inflammation connects it to the gut-brain axis, an increasingly important framework in depression research. Through these combined functions, TSPAN8 emerges as a plausible modulator of inflammatory, metabolic, and plasticity-related processes that may shape vulnerability to depression.

Shifting from inflammatory and barrier processes to cellular energetics, CHCHD10 is of particular interest because mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurring theme in depression research, especially in relation to impaired energy metabolism, oxidative stress, and reduced neuronal adaptability. Although the annotation provided here is concise, maintenance of mitochondrial organization and cristae structure is fundamentally important for oxidative phosphorylation and adenosine triphosphate production. In neurons, which are highly energy-dependent, disruption of mitochondrial architecture can impair synaptic transmission, plasticity, calcium buffering, and stress resilience. These processes are all relevant to depression, where abnormalities in bioenergetics and mitochondrial health have been reported in both central and peripheral tissues. Therefore, CHCHD10 stands out as a plausible contributor to depression-related cellular vulnerability through effects on mitochondrial integrity.

Related to this broader theme of cellular stress adaptation, RNASE1 is potentially relevant to depression because its functions are closely tied to cellular stress responses, ribonucleic acid metabolism, and redox regulation. Depression is strongly associated with chronic stress exposure, oxidative imbalance, and altered translational control. The stress-dependent relocalization of RNASE1 and its regulation of angiogenin are particularly noteworthy because angiogenin influences ribonucleic acid cleavage, cellular survival programs, and stress adaptation. By restraining the cytotoxic ribonuclease activity of ANG under basal conditions and altering this balance during stress, RNASE1 may help determine whether cells maintain homeostasis or enter maladaptive stress states. Its proposed role in redox homeostasis further increases its relevance, as oxidative stress is widely implicated in depression and may contribute to neuroprogression. While the link is less direct than for inflammatory or myelination-related proteins, RNASE1 stands out as a plausible mediator of stress-sensitive molecular pathways relevant to depressive illness.[[130]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [[131]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [[132]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [[133]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [[134]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [[135]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [[136]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [[137]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [[138]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170) 

In comparison with the preceding proteins, CKAP4 may have a more indirect connection to depression, but it remains noteworthy because it is a receptor involved in antiproliferative signaling and is linked to a FZD8-related ligand, suggesting possible interface with Wnt-related biology. Wnt and FZD signaling have been repeatedly implicated in neurodevelopment, adult neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and antidepressant response. Although the annotation here does not explicitly establish a neural role for CKAP4, proteins that influence antiproliferative pathways can be relevant to depression through effects on cellular turnover, tissue repair, and potentially neuroplasticity-related signaling cascades. Therefore, CKAP4 is best considered a secondary candidate whose relevance would depend on broader biological context beyond the present annotation.

Finally, CHGA is potentially relevant to depression because it participates in endocrine secretory granule biogenesis through a cyclic adenosine monophosphate-protein kinase A-SP1 pathway. This is important in light of the strong involvement of neuroendocrine dysregulation in depression, particularly altered hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity and changes in peptide hormone and neuropeptide secretion. Secretory granule formation is essential for proper storage and regulated release of signaling molecules in endocrine and neuroendocrine cells. Moreover, cyclic adenosine monophosphate-protein kinase A signaling is itself a well-established pathway in mood disorder biology and antidepressant action. Although the current annotation does not directly connect CHGA to the brain, its role in endocrine secretory function makes it a plausible, albeit indirect, contributor to depression-related neuroendocrine abnormalities.

### symbiont entry into host cell (GO:0046718) 

Symbiont entry into host cell refers to the biological process by which a non-host organism, or its genetic material, crosses the host plasma membrane and becomes established within the host cell. In the literature provided, this process is represented mainly by microbial or viral entry events that depend on specific host surface receptors, proteases, membrane remodeling, and immune tolerance mechanisms. Structural studies of poliovirus and coxsackievirus indicate that host cell entry is initiated by highly specific receptor binding at the viral capsid surface, which triggers conformational changes, uncoating, and release of the viral genome into the host cell, thereby completing the entry process [[146]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41484135) [[147]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33539764). Other studies extend this concept beyond pathogenic invasion to host-microbe interactions in which commensal or symbiotic organisms may shape host susceptibility to cellular entry by regulating host entry factors, such as angiotensin-converting enzyme two and transmembrane serine protease two, or by modulating extracellular protease balance. More broadly, the pathway is biologically linked to epithelial barrier integrity, immune sensing, cytokine activation, and blood-brain barrier function, because successful microbial entry into host cells can initiate systemic inflammation and tissue injury that propagate beyond the primary site of infection. Thus, although this pathway is classically defined at the level of cellular invasion, its physiological significance may extend to downstream effects on innate immunity, inflammatory signaling, vascular permeability, and neuroimmune communication.

Building on this mechanistic background, the available evidence does not support a direct, primary role for symbiont entry into host cell as a canonical depression pathway, but it does suggest an indirect and biologically plausible connection through infection-driven inflammation, host entry factor regulation, and blood-brain barrier disruption. Viral entry studies show that receptor-mediated invasion of host cells is the critical first step in infection by poliovirus and coxsackievirus, and blockade of this entry step can prevent downstream pathogenic consequences [[146]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41484135) [[147]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33539764). In the context of depression, this observation is relevant because infectious or post-infectious inflammatory states are increasingly recognized as contributors to depressive symptoms. A review of sepsis-associated blood-brain barrier dysfunction reports that systemic infection damages vascular endothelium and tight junctions, facilitates peripheral immune cell entry into the brain, activates glial cells, and promotes neuroinflammation; importantly, these processes are associated with long-term neuropsychiatric outcomes including depression [[148]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33319634). A further conceptual link is suggested by the discussion of angiotensin-converting enzyme two as a host entry factor for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two, where dysregulation of this entry-related axis is connected not only to inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and blood-brain barrier disruption, but also to depression and anxiety as part of neurological and neuropsychiatric disease manifestations [[149]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36836893). Consistent with this framework, one network pharmacology study on a traditional medicinal formulation proposes that preventing severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two entry into host cells may reduce infection-related inflammatory activation, while antidepressant benefit may arise through suppression of excessive cytokine signaling, thereby linking host cell entry events to depression through immune pathways rather than through a depression-specific cellular mechanism. Overall, the available evidence indicates that this pathway may be related to depression chiefly when host cell entry of viruses or other microbes initiates systemic and central nervous system inflammation, compromises barrier function, and amplifies cytokine-mediated neurobiological changes that are known to promote depressive phenotypes, rather than because symbiont entry itself is an established core molecular pathway of depression.[[146]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41484135) [[147]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33539764) [[148]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33319634) [[149]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36836893) 

With this broader interpretation in mind, the enrichment results provide a more focused view of how this process may intersect with depression-associated biology. There were 11 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of symbiont entry into host cell, a biological process centered on the crossing of the host plasma membrane by a non-host organism or its genetic material and the subsequent establishment within the host cell. In this context, the pathway is supported by mechanistic evidence showing that host cell entry depends on quantitatively important molecular determinants, including specific surface receptor engagement, protease-dependent priming, membrane remodeling, and immune tolerance mechanisms. The literature further indicates that receptor-guided viral entry is a highly ordered multistep process in which capsid binding, conformational rearrangement, uncoating, and genome release occur sequentially, thereby defining a complete cellular entry program [[146]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41484135) [[147]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33539764). Beyond direct invasion, this pathway has broader biological relevance because host-microbe interactions can regulate major host entry factors such as angiotensin-converting enzyme two and transmembrane serine protease two, while also altering extracellular protease balance, epithelial barrier integrity, cytokine activation, vascular permeability, blood-brain barrier function, and neuroimmune communication. Given that the enriched set contains 11 proteins, the signal is consistent with a focused but biologically meaningful host entry- and inflammation-related module in depression, particularly in view of the established links between systemic inflammation, barrier dysfunction, and central nervous system immune signaling in depressive pathology. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 11 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct inspection of network connectivity and evidence structure.

![PPI Network](imgs/aa9472eb-509e-4363-a2fc-d92fb4a0cea0.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=F086FC4DA5A419C3)

To clarify the biological contribution of this enriched set, the significant proteins are considered individually below. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, LGALS1 is one of the most compelling candidates for relevance to depression because its annotated functions converge on immune regulation, lymphocyte survival, and inflammatory T-cell polarization. Depression is increasingly linked to chronic low-grade inflammation, altered adaptive immunity, and abnormal cytokine signaling. In this context, the ability of galectin-1 to induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T helper seventeen differentiation is particularly notable, because T helper seventeen-associated immune responses and broader immune disequilibrium have been implicated in neuroinflammatory states that may influence mood, stress responsivity, and synaptic function. Its inhibition of cluster of differentiation forty-five phosphatase activity and consequent effects on Lyn-dependent signaling further suggest that LGALS1 can reshape immune-cell activation thresholds. Collectively, these properties make LGALS1 relevant to depression not necessarily as a classical neurotransmission molecule, but as an immunomodulatory factor that could influence the inflammatory milieu associated with depressive pathophysiology.[[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

In a closely related manner, LGALS9 also appears notable because its functions directly implicate immune suppression and cytokine regulation, both of which are highly relevant to current inflammatory models of depression. The suppression of interferon gamma production by natural killer cells is especially important, as interferon gamma is a central immunoregulatory cytokine with downstream effects on neuroimmune communication, microglial activation, and tryptophan metabolism pathways that have been linked to depressive symptoms. Its anti-angiogenic activity may also be of interest, given emerging evidence that vascular dysfunction and impaired neurovascular support can contribute to stress-related brain changes. Although the annotation is relatively concise, LGALS9 is notable as a plausible regulator of the immune-neuroendocrine interface, which is increasingly recognized as central to depression biology.

Extending from lectin-mediated immune regulation to matrix-dependent signaling, ITGAV is highly relevant to depression because it sits at the intersection of extracellular matrix signaling, neuroinflammation, vascular biology, and transforming growth factor beta regulation. Of particular importance is the documented role of alpha-V-containing integrins in activating transforming growth factor beta one from its latent complex [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [[8]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859). Transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major regulator of immune tolerance, glial behavior, tissue remodeling, and blood-brain barrier-associated processes, all of which have been implicated in depressive disorders. In addition, ITGAV-mediated interactions with extracellular matrix proteins and growth factor pathways suggest broader roles in cell adhesion, angiogenesis, and repair responses, processes that may affect synaptic plasticity and stress-induced structural remodeling in the brain. The involvement of ITGAV:ITGB3 in interleukin one beta-related signaling is also noteworthy, because interleukin one beta is one of the most consistently implicated inflammatory mediators in depression. Thus, ITGAV stands out as a multifunctional upstream regulator with plausible links to both inflammatory and neuroplasticity-related mechanisms of depression.[[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [[150]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [[8]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [[151]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [[152]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

Shifting from extracellular matrix signaling to immune-cell contact dynamics, NECTIN2 is of interest in depression primarily because of its role in immune-cell communication and cytotoxic lymphocyte activation. Depression has been associated not only with inflammatory cytokine abnormalities but also with altered natural killer cell function and broader disturbances in cellular immunity. NECTIN2 contributes to immune synapse formation and downstream activation of phosphoinositide three-kinase, phospholipase C gamma one, extracellular signal-regulated kinase, and protein kinase B pathways, which are central signaling modules in both immune responses and cellular stress adaptation. While the annotation does not directly place NECTIN2 in neurobiology, its regulation of natural killer cell and cytotoxic T-cell activity suggests potential relevance to peripheral immune states that may influence brain function through cytokine signaling and neuroimmune crosstalk. Therefore, NECTIN2 may be considered a moderate-priority candidate linking immune surveillance and lymphocyte activation to depression-related systemic immune alterations.[[153]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8673704) [[154]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9712030) [[155]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26755705) [[156]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31253644) [[157]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30591568) 

In comparison with these more strongly immune-regulatory candidates, SIGLEC1 appears less directly connected to depression, although it may still be relevant in specific inflammatory contexts because it participates in dendritic-cell interactions with viral particles. Infection and post-infectious immune activation are recognized contributors to depressive symptomatology in some patients, and dendritic-cell activation can shape systemic cytokine responses that secondarily affect the brain. Thus, SIGLEC1 may be relevant in contexts where depression is associated with viral infection, chronic immune activation, or inflammatory sequelae of host-pathogen interactions. However, based on the provided annotation, its connection appears more indirect and context-dependent than that of LGALS1, LGALS9, or ITGAV.

Finally, based strictly on the provided functional annotation, SMPD1 does not emerge as a strong candidate for meaningful relevance to depression in this dataset, because it is explicitly described as catalytically inactive. Although sphingolipid metabolism can be important in neurobiology and psychiatric disease, the current annotation does not support an active mechanistic role for this specific protein entry. Therefore, compared with the other proteins listed, SMPD1 appears to have the weakest immediate interpretive connection to depression.

### lipid localization (GO:0010876) 

Lipid localization refers to the set of biological processes that transport lipids to defined cellular or tissue compartments, retain them there, and dynamically redistribute them when physiological conditions change. This pathway includes the movement and compartmentalization of membrane phospholipids, sphingolipids, cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains, fatty acids, and bioactive lipid mediators across organelles, membranes, endosomes, synapses, glial membranes, and extracellular interfaces. In the nervous system, lipid localization is especially important because the functional properties of neurons and glial cells depend strongly on membrane composition and on the spatial organization of lipids within the plasma membrane and intracellular trafficking systems. Proper lipid localization regulates receptor clustering, membrane fluidity, vesicular trafficking, synaptic pruning, neurotransmitter receptor delivery, signal transduction, inflammatory signaling, oxidative vulnerability, and the generation of lipid-derived mediators. Disturbance of lipid localization can therefore alter how signaling proteins are positioned in lipid raft domains, how synaptic proteins are trafficked through endosomal compartments, how microglia interact with neuronal membranes, and how inflammatory or pro-resolving lipid molecules act within mood-related brain regions. In the context of depression, this pathway appears relevant because depressive pathology has been linked to abnormal membrane microenvironment organization, disordered phospholipid synthesis and localization, neuroinflammation-associated lipid metabolic disruption, region-specific changes in brain lipid distribution, and altered availability or action of signaling lipids that modulate stress responses, neuroplasticity, and immune activity. 

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that altered lipid localization may be mechanistically linked to depression through convergent effects on membrane signaling, synaptic plasticity, microglial function, neuroinflammation, and lipid mediator biology. A particularly direct line of evidence comes from postmortem brain tissue showing that in unipolar depression, the stimulatory guanine nucleotide-binding protein alpha subunit is preferentially localized to lipid raft membrane domains in the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, where it is less able to activate adenylyl cyclase, whereas antidepressant treatment is thought to reverse this membrane redistribution, implying that depression may be associated with maladaptive localization of signaling proteins within lipid microenvironments [[158]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18354007). Relatedly, neuronal studies demonstrate that palmitoylation-dependent targeting of A-kinase anchoring protein seventy-nine and one hundred fifty to postsynaptic lipid rafts and dendritic recycling endosomes is required for glutamate receptor trafficking and long-term potentiation and long-term depression mechanisms, supporting the possibility that disturbed lipid-dependent subcellular targeting can impair synaptic adaptations relevant to mood regulation [[159]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22623657). Evidence from microglia further strengthens this line of reasoning: reduced serine incorporator two expression in microglia from bipolar depression models disrupts serine-related phospholipid synthesis in microglial membranes, impairs complement receptor three membrane localization, weakens synaptic pruning, and promotes depression-like behaviors, thereby directly connecting phospholipid localization at the microglial membrane to depressive phenotypes [[160]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40920917). More broadly, reviews of brain membrane lipids and of the endocannabinoid and endovanilloid system suggest that the localization and composition of lipids in neuronal membranes shape receptor function, monoaminergic signaling, stress-axis regulation, and neuroplasticity, all of which are central biological domains in depression [[161]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25542508) [[162]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25426013). Several studies also indicate that depression-related states may involve broader disturbances in lipid distribution and metabolism within the brain: frequent fried food exposure and chronic acrylamide treatment induce anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors together with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor signaling-associated lipid metabolic disorder in brain tissue [[163]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37094155), while mass spectrometry imaging of hippocampal subregions in a depression-related disease model identifies localized alterations in phosphatidylinositols, phosphatidylserines, phosphatidylethanolamines, and sulfatides, indicating that region-specific lipid localization changes accompany depressive pathology [[164]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40787721). Additional support comes from studies showing that depression-associated conditions are linked to fatty acid peroxidation and oxylipin disturbances along the gut-brain axis [[165]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40450088), whereas specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators such as resolvin E one exert antidepressant-like effects in the medial prefrontal cortex and dentate gyrus, implying that the localization and action of protective lipid signals in discrete brain regions may counter depressive behavior [[166]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38945902). Taken together, these findings support a model in which depression may be associated not only with altered lipid abundance, but also with abnormal spatial organization of lipids and lipid-dependent proteins across neuronal and glial membranes, membrane microdomains, and brain subregions, thereby potentially disrupting intracellular signaling, synaptic remodeling, immune surveillance, and inflammatory resolution.[[163]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37094155) [[160]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40920917) [[158]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18354007) [[159]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22623657) [[162]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25426013) [[161]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25542508) [[164]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40787721) [[166]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38945902) [[165]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40450088) 

Consistent with this literature-based context, there were 6 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of lipid localization. This enrichment is biologically notable because lipid localization governs the transport, retention, and redistribution of multiple lipid classes across cellular compartments, and in the nervous system even modest disruption of these spatial processes can influence membrane composition, receptor positioning, vesicular trafficking, inflammatory signaling, and lipid mediator availability across neurons and glial cells. In depression, the relevance of this pathway is further supported by convergent evidence linking altered membrane microenvironment organization, disturbed phospholipid handling, neuroinflammation-related lipid dysregulation, and region-specific shifts in brain lipid distribution to stress responsiveness, neuroplasticity, and immune signaling. Taken together, these observations suggest that this 6-protein enriched set may map onto a mechanistic axis with direct pathophysiological relevance.

The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 6 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration and evidence review.

![PPI Network](imgs/5f5929e4-fd8b-47ef-9bef-7035f327f3b3.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=DC2AC02AE605521B)

With this network context in place, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help clarify how lipid localization-related biology could connect to depression. We introduce these proteins in detail below.

Among the proteins listed, MDK stands out as highly relevant to depression because it lies at the intersection of several biological processes strongly implicated in depressive pathophysiology, namely neuroinflammation, impaired neuroplasticity, altered neuronal survival, and dysfunctional tissue repair. MDK has direct neurotrophic actions in the brain, including promotion of neural precursor cell survival and growth, neuronal migration, neurite outgrowth, and neuronal survival through receptors such as PTPRZ1, LRP1, syndecans/glypicans, and integrins, suggesting a potential role in maintaining neural circuit integrity and adaptive plasticity, processes that are frequently disrupted in depression [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [[14]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [[19]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439). At the same time, MDK is a potent immunomodulatory factor: it recruits neutrophils and macrophages to inflammatory sites, induces chemokine expression, and shapes adaptive immunity by suppressing tolerogenic dendritic cells while promoting T-cell expansion and T helper cell one polarization [[17]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [[18]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [[16]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438). This dual role is particularly important because contemporary models of depression emphasize reciprocal interactions between peripheral inflammation and brain function. Persistent inflammatory signaling can alter neurotransmission, reduce neurogenesis, and impair stress resilience; therefore, a molecule such as MDK, which can amplify inflammatory cell recruitment yet also support cell survival and regeneration, may contribute to both maladaptive and compensatory responses relevant to depressive illness. Its activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase, phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B, angiogenic, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related pathways further strengthens its potential relevance, as these signaling cascades are linked to stress responses, synaptic remodeling, and structural brain changes observed in mood disorders [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [[15]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519). Overall, MDK is notable because it mechanistically connects immune activation with neurodevelopmental and neurorestorative pathways, making it a plausible contributor to depression-related changes in brain plasticity and inflammatory tone.[[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [[17]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [[14]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [[19]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) [[15]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [[18]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [[16]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

In a related but distinct way, TREM2 further extends this theme by highlighting the possible contribution of microglial and innate immune processes within the same enriched pathway context.

TREM2 is especially compelling in the context of depression because it directly implicates microglial biology, which has emerged as a central component of depression-associated neuroimmune dysfunction. Through its partnership with TYROBP, TREM2 is required for microglial phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons, indicating an essential role in cellular debris clearance and maintenance of neural homeostasis [[84]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241). Dysregulated microglial phagocytosis has been proposed to contribute to aberrant synaptic remodeling and neuronal vulnerability in depression, particularly under chronic stress or inflammatory conditions. In addition, TREM2-TYROBP signaling contributes to the control of microglial superoxide production and can promote pro-inflammatory responses after nerve injury, accelerating neuronal degeneration [[89]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [[90]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660). These functions are highly relevant because oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and subtle neurodegenerative-like changes are repeatedly observed in subsets of patients with major depressive disorder. TREM2 also influences dendritic cell maturation, chemokine receptor regulation, and anti-inflammatory interleukin ten-associated programs in certain immune contexts, indicating that it may shape both central and peripheral immune states [[91]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958). This combination of homeostatic and inflammatory functions makes TREM2 particularly important: depending on context, it may either protect the brain by facilitating clearance and immune regulation or contribute to pathological neuroinflammation and neuronal injury. Such context dependence mirrors current views of depression as a heterogeneous disorder in which maladaptive immune activation and altered glial function play major mechanistic roles. Therefore, TREM2 is a standout candidate for linking innate immune signaling, microglial activation states, oxidative injury, and neural circuit alterations relevant to depressive symptoms.[[84]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [[89]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [[91]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [[90]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660)

### Cytokines and inflammatory response (WP:WP530) 

The cytokine and inflammatory response pathway comprises a coordinated network of immune signaling molecules, their receptors, intracellular transcriptional regulators, inflammasome machinery, and cellular effectors that together detect danger signals and orchestrate host defense, tissue adaptation, and repair. Within this pathway, proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin one beta, interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interferon gamma, interleukin seventeen alpha, and chemokines including C C motif chemokine ligand two and C C motif chemokine ligand four promote leukocyte activation, endothelial signaling, glial reactivity, and transcriptional programs driven by mediators such as nuclear factor kappa B and mitogen activated protein kinase signaling. At the same time, counterregulatory components, including interleukin ten, interleukin one receptor antagonist, regulatory T cells, and other compensatory immune mechanisms, help restrain excessive inflammatory activation. In the nervous system, peripheral inflammatory signals can influence the brain through humoral, neural, and cellular routes, leading to microglial activation, altered synaptic plasticity, disturbed neuroendocrine regulation, and changes in monoamine and tryptophan metabolism. Inflammasome related processes, especially those involving NLR family pyrin domain containing three, caspase one, interleukin one beta, and interleukin eighteen, may further amplify neuroinflammatory tone. Taken together, this pathway can be viewed not only as a canonical immune defense system but also as a major interface between stress, sleep disturbance, metabolic dysfunction, medical comorbidity, and brain circuits that regulate mood, motivation, reward, and cognition.

Against this biological background, the collected literature indicates that the cytokine and inflammatory response pathway is mechanistically and clinically linked to depression through both peripheral immune activation and central neuroinflammatory signaling. Across major depression and late life depression, patients show higher circulating inflammatory mediators, including interleukin one receptor antagonist, interleukin seventeen alpha, interferon gamma, C C motif chemokine ligand two, and C C motif chemokine ligand four, supporting the view that depression is frequently accompanied by a measurable inflammatory state rather than being exclusively a neurotransmitter disorder [[167]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39922907) [[168]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33961966). This inflammatory burden appears especially relevant to a biologically distinct subgroup of depressed patients, because an inflammatory subtype of depression has been proposed in which elevated immune markers are associated with symptoms such as anhedonia, fatigue, and psychomotor slowing, and may predict differential treatment response [[169]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40329642) [[168]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33961966). Evidence suggestive of causality is strengthened by experimental inflammatory challenge: in older adults, endotoxin exposure induced larger increases in depressed mood and depressive symptoms in those with insomnia, even though cytokine induction was similar across groups, indicating that vulnerability to depression may arise from heightened affective sensitivity to inflammatory signals rather than from absolute cytokine magnitude alone [[170]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40668551). At the mechanistic level, inflammatory cytokines engage intracellular pathways highly relevant to depression, including nuclear factor kappa B, mitogen activated protein kinase signaling, insulin receptor substrate signaling, and inflammasome biology; notably, in bipolar depression, inflammatory biotypes moderated response to tumor necrosis factor alpha blockade, and improvement in anhedonia was associated with changes in neuronal extracellular vesicle markers linked to nuclear factor kappa B and related inflammatory cascades [[171]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33658605). Convergent preclinical studies further support this framework by showing that chronic stress produces depressive like behavior together with increased interleukin one beta, interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and interferon gamma, reduced interleukin ten, and microglial polarization toward a proinflammatory state, whereas interventions such as running exercise restore microglial balance and suppress hippocampal neuroinflammation through adiponectin receptor signaling and downstream adenosine monophosphate activated protein kinase, nuclear factor kappa B, and signal transducer and activator of transcription three pathways [[172]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38361125) [[173]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35219870). Additional evidence implicates inflammasome signaling and immune cell phenotypes, as the silent information regulator one and NLR family pyrin domain containing three axis has been proposed as a regulator of neuroinflammation relevant to depression, and postpartum depression models show that reducing interleukin one beta and interleukin six while restoring regulatory T cells ameliorates depressive phenotypes [[174]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37507744) [[175]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27143890).
