Clinical modifiers such as obesity, diabetes, insomnia, multiple sclerosis, and spinal cord injury further reinforce this relationship by showing that stronger inflammatory cytokine profiles accompany greater depressive severity, suicidality, or persistent mood symptoms [[176]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38022570) [[177]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31049023) [[178]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34589900) [[179]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30659938). Taken together, these studies support a model in which dysregulated cytokine signaling, insufficient compensatory anti inflammatory control, microglial activation, and downstream effects on reward, stress, and neuroplasticity pathways may contribute substantially to the onset, heterogeneity, and treatment responsiveness of depression.[[171]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33658605) [[170]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40668551) [[167]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39922907) [[172]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38361125) [[174]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37507744) [[178]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34589900) [[168]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33961966) [[177]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31049023) [[175]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27143890) [[179]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30659938) [[176]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38022570) [[169]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40329642) [[173]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35219870) 

Consistent with this literature based context, there were 6 depression associated proteins significantly enriched in the cytokine and inflammatory response pathway, indicating that this immune related pathway captures a measurable fraction of the analyzed disease linked protein set. This pathway comprises a broad signaling architecture that includes proinflammatory cytokines, chemokines, receptors, transcriptional regulators, inflammasome components, and compensatory anti inflammatory mechanisms, and its enrichment in a 6 protein set is consistent with the well documented contribution of inflammatory signaling to depression through effects on microglial activation, synaptic plasticity, neuroendocrine regulation, and monoamine and tryptophan metabolism. Because the enriched pathway explicitly integrates interleukin one beta, interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, interferon gamma, interleukin seventeen alpha, C C motif chemokine ligand two, C C motif chemokine ligand four, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, mitogen activated protein kinase signaling, and NLR family pyrin domain containing three inflammasome related processes, the identification of 6 associated proteins may support a biologically coherent inflammatory signature connecting peripheral immune activation with mood, motivation, reward, and cognition relevant to depression.

### Pancreatic cancer subtypes (WP:WP5390) 

Pancreatic cancer subtypes refers to the biologically distinct molecular, epigenetic, proteomic, developmental, and microenvironmental states that exist within pancreatic malignancies, especially pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Across the cited studies, this pathway is not a single linear signaling cascade, but rather a disease-organizing framework in which tumors segregate into recurrent subtype programs, most prominently a more classical epithelial state and a more basal-like or squamous or mesenchymal aggressive state, with additional intermediate, stromal, and immune-associated variants. These subtype states are defined by differences in chromatin organization, histone modification, deoxyribonucleic acid methylation, enhancer and super-enhancer usage, transcription factor activity, developmental lineage programs, oncogenic signaling, stromal composition, and immune communication. Epigenomic work has shown that pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma subtypes possess distinct promoter, enhancer, super-enhancer, euchromatin, and heterochromatin landscapes, and that these chromatin states are linked to differences in aggressiveness and survival, indicating that subtype identity is deeply rooted in transcriptional regulation and cellular plasticity rather than only mutational status alone [[180]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29773832). Proteogenomic analysis further supports the existence of biologically distinct subtype groupings with differential activation of Wnt signaling, Notch signaling, and phosphoinositide 3-kinase to mechanistic target of rapamycin signaling, suggesting that subtype identity influences both cell-intrinsic growth programs and therapeutic vulnerabilities [[181]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34506537). Additional studies indicate that subtype architecture extends beyond malignant epithelial cells to include coordinated stromal and immune states, including extracellular matrix-rich versus immune-enriched stromal programs, myofibroblastic versus inflammatory fibroblast states, and subtype-specific secreted factors that shape immunosuppressive myeloid and lymphoid niches. Single-cell and spatial studies also suggest that subtype composition can coexist within the same tumor, can emerge from common precursor populations, and may reflect reactivation of developmental endodermal programs. Thus, the pancreatic cancer subtype pathway is best understood as a multidimensional system linking tumor cell state, tumor microenvironment, inflammatory signaling, metabolic stress, and clinical outcome.

Against this biological background, the possible relationship between pancreatic cancer subtypes and depression appears to be indirect but still biologically meaningful.

The relationship between pancreatic cancer subtypes and depression appears to be indirect but biologically meaningful, operating through inflammatory, metabolic, neuroendocrine, and tumor microenvironment mechanisms rather than through a depression-specific oncogenic pathway. Clinically, depression is more severe in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma than in patients with other pancreatic tumor types, and greater lifetime stressor exposure is associated with higher odds of clinically significant depressive symptoms, indicating that pancreatic tumor biology and psychosocial burden intersect in shaping depressive outcomes [[182]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41062956). Mechanistically, the most relevant evidence suggests that aggressive pancreatic cancer states are accompanied by inflammatory and metabolic programs that are also highly plausible drivers of depression biology. In the study examining cachexia and depression in pancreatic cancer, depression was associated with elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, increased colony stimulating factor three expression, enrichment of tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin six to janus kinase to signal transducer and activator of transcription three signaling, interferon responses, lipid metabolism pathways, cytokine elevation including tumor necrosis factor and interleukin one beta, T cell exclusion, and enrichment of stress-related genes such as thioredoxin interacting protein and growth differentiation factor fifteen, together with cortisol-regulated transcriptional programs. These findings support a model in which depressive symptoms in pancreatic cancer are linked to a myeloid-inflamed, immunosuppressive, metabolically stressed tumor ecosystem that can promote systemic inflammation and neuroimmune dysregulation. This model is highly consistent with the broader pancreatic subtype literature showing that aggressive basal-like or squamous or mesenchymal states are characterized by distinct epigenetic wiring, inflammatory signaling, immune remodeling, and stromal communication networks, all of which could amplify circulating cytokines, sickness behavior, cachexia, and depression vulnerability [[180]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29773832) [[181]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34506537). Studies of subtype-specific tumor microenvironments further indicate that pancreatic cancer subtypes differ in secreted factors and immune cell organization, especially in their interactions with immunosuppressive myeloid populations, providing a plausible bridge between subtype biology and depression-related systemic inflammation. Therefore, although pancreatic cancer subtypes were not originally defined as a depression pathway, the available evidence suggests that more aggressive subtype states may increase depression risk by fostering chronic inflammatory signaling, metabolic stress, endocrine stress responses, and debilitating symptom clusters such as cachexia, whereas subtype-informed clinical care may help identify patients at greatest risk for depression and in need of integrated psychosocial and anti-inflammatory support [[182]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41062956).[[180]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29773832) [[181]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34506537) [[182]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41062956) 

Building on this conceptual link between subtype biology and depression-related processes, the enrichment analysis provides a more focused view of the proteins represented in this pathway.

There were 11 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of pancreatic cancer subtypes, a multidimensional disease-organizing framework that captures biologically distinct molecular, epigenetic, proteomic, developmental, stromal, and immune states within pancreatic malignancies. This enrichment indicates that the analyzed protein set converges on a pathway characterized by at least 2 major recurrent tumor cell programs, namely a more classical epithelial state and a more basal-like or squamous or mesenchymal aggressive state, together with additional intermediate, stromal, and immune-associated variants. The biological relevance of this pathway is supported by evidence showing that subtype identity is associated with distinct promoter, enhancer, super-enhancer, euchromatin, and heterochromatin landscapes, and that these chromatin differences are linked to variation in tumor aggressiveness and survival [[180]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29773832). Further support comes from proteogenomic analysis demonstrating differential activation across multiple signaling systems, including Wnt signaling, Notch signaling, and phosphoinositide 3-kinase to mechanistic target of rapamycin signaling, which collectively indicate that subtype identity shapes both intrinsic growth behavior and therapeutic vulnerability [[181]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34506537). In addition to malignant epithelial programs, this pathway also integrates extracellular matrix-rich versus immune-enriched stromal states, myofibroblastic versus inflammatory fibroblast programs, and subtype-specific secreted factors that remodel myeloid and lymphoid niches, thereby linking tumor cell plasticity, inflammatory signaling, metabolic stress, microenvironmental organization, and clinical outcome into a single enriched biological context.

With this network context in place, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, AREG is one of the most plausibly connected to depression because epidermal growth factor receptor signaling intersects with neurotrophic support, glial biology, tissue repair, and neuroinflammatory responses. Its documented mitogenic activity toward astrocytes is particularly relevant, as astrocytic dysfunction has been increasingly implicated in major depressive disorder, including impaired synaptic support, altered glutamate homeostasis, and abnormal neuroimmune signaling. In addition, growth factor pathways are broadly linked to stress adaptation and structural plasticity in corticolimbic circuits that are disrupted in depression. Although AREG is not a canonical depression gene, its role as an epidermal growth factor receptor ligand suggests potential relevance to mechanisms involving glial reactivity, cellular resilience, and inflammatory remodeling, all of which are biologically meaningful in depressive pathophysiology.

In a related but somewhat broader mechanistic sense, TSPAN8 may be especially informative because it appears to connect several systems that have each been implicated in depression biology.

TSPAN8 stands out as the most mechanistically informative candidate in relation to depression because it converges on several biological systems strongly implicated in the disorder. First, its promotion of ADAM17-mediated tumor necrosis factor alpha processing links it directly to inflammatory signaling, and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine activity is a well-established feature in a subset of patients with depression. Second, its effects on mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2 and AKT1 signaling are notable because mechanistic target of rapamycin pathway dysfunction has been associated with impaired synaptic plasticity, stress susceptibility, and antidepressant response. Third, its role in maintaining intestinal epithelial barrier integrity and limiting intestinal inflammation is highly relevant to the gut-brain axis, which has emerged as an important framework for understanding depression through mechanisms involving barrier dysfunction, immune activation, and microbiome-host interactions. Finally, modulation of endothelin biology may also be relevant, given growing evidence that vascular and neurovascular dysfunction can contribute to depressive symptoms. Taken together, TSPAN8 connects inflammatory, metabolic, barrier, and signaling mechanisms that are all highly pertinent to depression biology.

By comparison, the connection of AGR3 to depression appears more indirect, but it may still be biologically noteworthy when considered through the lens of cellular signaling.

AGR3 has a less direct connection to depression than AREG or TSPAN8, but it remains potentially relevant because calcium signaling is a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability, neurotransmitter release, and intracellular stress responses. The currently described function of AGR3 is centered on airway epithelial physiology rather than the nervous system; however, the mention of intracellular calcium regulation makes it biologically interesting in a broader context. Disturbances in calcium-dependent signaling have been associated with mood disorders, including altered synaptic transmission and stress-related cellular dysfunction. Therefore, while current evidence from the provided function does not support AGR3 as a strong depression-linked candidate, its involvement in calcium regulation suggests a plausible, albeit indirect, mechanistic relevance.

A similar pattern of indirect relevance is also seen for TFF2, although in this case the potential connection appears to center more clearly on gastrointestinal and systemic pathways.

TFF2 is potentially relevant to depression primarily through the gut-brain axis. Although its described function is gastrointestinal, it contributes to mucosal protection and mucus stability, processes that are important for maintaining gastrointestinal homeostasis. Depression is increasingly associated with altered gut physiology, low-grade inflammation, and bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system. Proteins involved in mucus barrier integrity may influence host-microbe interactions and inflammatory tone, which in turn can affect mood-related neuroimmune pathways. Thus, TFF2 is not a direct neuropsychiatric factor, but its role in gastric and mucosal defense may be meaningful in the context of systemic and gut-mediated contributors to depression.

Finally, LGALS4 can be interpreted within the same general framework of barrier integrity and immune regulation, which may provide an additional indirect route linking this protein to depression-related biology.

LGALS4 may be relevant to depression because galectins and cell-adhesion-related molecules can influence epithelial integrity, immune signaling, and intercellular communication. Its putative role in adherens junction assembly suggests possible importance in barrier biology, which is increasingly studied in relation to depression, especially in the context of intestinal permeability and peripheral inflammation. Although the provided function does not indicate a direct neural role, junctional stability and glycan-mediated signaling can shape inflammatory environments that may secondarily affect brain function. Therefore, LGALS4 is best considered an indirect candidate whose relevance to depression would most likely arise through barrier and immunoregulatory mechanisms.

### Post-translational protein phosphorylation (REAC:R-HSA-8957275) 

Post-translational protein phosphorylation is a reversible regulatory process in which phosphate groups are covalently added to specific amino acid residues, most commonly serine, threonine, or tyrosine, after a protein has been synthesized. This modification is catalyzed by protein kinases and reversed by protein phosphatases, thereby creating a dynamic molecular switch that can rapidly alter protein activity, localization, stability, intermolecular binding, and degradation. In the nervous system, post-translational protein phosphorylation is central to synaptic transmission, receptor trafficking, cytoskeletal remodeling, neuronal excitability, intracellular calcium signaling, and activity-dependent gene regulation. It is especially important for long-term potentiation and long-term depression, the major forms of synaptic plasticity that underlie learning, memory, and adaptive behavioral responses. The pathway also operates in close coordination with other post-translational modifications, including O-linked beta-N-acetylglucosamine addition, palmitoylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination, meaning that phosphorylation often functions as part of a broader signaling code rather than as an isolated event. In brain circuits relevant to mood regulation, such as the medial prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus, phosphorylation-dependent control of glutamate receptors, scaffold proteins, transporters, and signaling enzymes governs the strength and structure of excitatory synapses. Because depressive illness is strongly associated with maladaptive stress responses, impaired synaptic plasticity, altered energy metabolism, and disrupted communication between neuronal and inflammatory systems, abnormalities in post-translational protein phosphorylation are well positioned to contribute to disease mechanisms and treatment responses.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature indicates that post-translational protein phosphorylation is closely related to depression because it regulates the synaptic and cellular processes that are repeatedly disrupted in depressive illness. A multi-tissue proteomic integration study in patients with depression found that post-translational modifications, particularly phosphorylation, were common among dysregulated proteins, with brain networks enriched for synapse, neuron, respiration, and cell adhesion functions, supporting the view that phosphorylation abnormalities may represent a systems-level feature of depression rather than an isolated molecular event [[183]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41611983). More directly, a phosphoproteomic study of chronic stress-induced depression in mice showed widespread phosphorylation changes in the medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens, with synaptic transmission-related signaling emerging as a shared abnormality; importantly, many stress-induced phosphorylation changes were reversed by ketamine, linking phosphorylation remodeling to both disease pathogenesis and rapid antidepressant response [[184]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32317933). Mechanistically, several cited studies show how phosphorylation controls long-term synaptic depression and excitatory receptor trafficking, processes highly relevant to the synaptic weakening observed in depression. For example, phosphorylation state changes in alpha-amino-three-hydroxy-five-methyl-four-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor subunits and associated proteins regulate receptor internalization and long-term depression, while calcium and calmodulin dependent protein kinase signaling and scaffold protein remodeling contribute to structural synaptic depression and dendritic spine shrinkage [[185]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27624155) [[186]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29196604) [[187]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29414768) [[188]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31394063) [[189]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41268362). Additional evidence suggests that phosphorylation-dependent regulation extends to depression risk molecules: the neutral amino acid transporter solute carrier family six member fifteen, genetically linked to major depressive disorder, contains prominent phosphorylation sites and is predicted to be controlled by kinases and signaling networks implicated in stress responses and synaptic plasticity, including the erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase signaling pathway [[190]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41649124). The pathway is further connected to depression through crosstalk with other post-translational modifications. O-linked beta-N-acetylglucosamine addition occurs on serine residues that often overlap with phosphorylation sites, and experimentally increasing this modification induces a novel form of long-term depression at hippocampal synapses, disrupts long-term potentiation, and impairs recognition memory, demonstrating how competition or interaction between these modifications can bias synapses toward depression-like weakening of connectivity [[191]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24381264) [[192]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28760863). Taken together, these studies support a coherent model in which abnormal post-translational protein phosphorylation may contribute to depression by reshaping glutamatergic signaling, stress-responsive circuit plasticity, dendritic structure, and possibly transporter and metabolic regulation, while successful antidepressant intervention may in part act by normalizing these phosphorylation-dependent signaling states.[[183]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41611983) [[184]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32317933) [[185]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27624155) [[186]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29196604) [[187]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29414768) [[188]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31394063) [[189]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41268362) [[190]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41649124) [[191]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24381264) [[192]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28760863) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment results provide a pathway-level view of how these mechanisms may be represented in the analyzed depression-associated protein set. There were 11 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of post-translational protein phosphorylation, indicating that this regulatory process captures a substantial functional signal within the analyzed protein set. Post-translational protein phosphorylation represents a reversible molecular mechanism in which phosphate groups are added to specific amino acid residues after protein synthesis and removed by counteracting enzymes, thereby creating a dynamic regulatory system that can rapidly modify protein activity, intracellular localization, molecular stability, intermolecular interaction strength, and degradation rate. In the context of depression, the enrichment of 11 proteins in this pathway is biologically notable because phosphorylation-dependent signaling is deeply involved in synaptic transmission, receptor trafficking, cytoskeletal remodeling, neuronal excitability, intracellular calcium signaling, and activity-dependent gene regulation, all of which are processes strongly implicated in stress adaptation, mood regulation, and maladaptive neuroplasticity. The pathway is also especially relevant to long-term potentiation and long-term depression, two major forms of synaptic plasticity that support learning, memory, and behavioral adaptation, and disturbances in these phosphorylation-governed processes may plausibly contribute to the impaired synaptic function, altered circuit connectivity, disrupted energy metabolism, and abnormal neuroimmune communication observed in depressive illness. In addition, because phosphorylation acts in coordination with other post-translational modifications, including O-linked beta-N-acetylglucosamine addition, palmitoylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination, the enrichment of these 11 proteins suggests that depression-related molecular pathology may involve not a single isolated signaling event, but a broader regulatory code affecting excitatory synapses in key mood-related brain regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus.

With this network context in place, the following section introduces the proteins identified as significant in the function enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance in a cautious, evidence-based manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, LGALS1 stands out as one of the most plausibly connected to depression because its annotated functions converge on immune regulation, inflammatory T-cell biology, and cell survival pathways. Depression is increasingly understood to involve immune dysregulation and low-grade inflammation in at least a substantial subset of patients, with altered T-cell phenotypes and pro-inflammatory signaling frequently implicated in pathophysiology. The ability of galectin-1 to induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T helper seventeen differentiation suggests a potentially important role in shaping inflammatory tone. Because T helper seventeen-related cytokine programs have been associated with neuroinflammation, stress susceptibility, and altered neuroimmune communication, LGALS1 may be relevant to depression through modulation of peripheral immune responses that secondarily influence brain function. Its broader effects on apoptosis, proliferation, and differentiation further support possible roles in tissue remodeling and neuroimmune homeostasis, making it one of the most biologically compelling candidates in this list.[[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

In a related but more systemic direction, several of the next proteins point toward endocrine, metabolic, and growth factor signaling processes that may intersect with depression biology. FGF23 is of particular interest because the function provided explicitly links it to Klotho biology and inhibition of insulin-like growth factor one signaling, both of which are highly relevant to systemic aging, metabolic regulation, and brain health. Depression has strong mechanistic intersections with accelerated biological aging, endocrine dysfunction, and altered metabolic signaling. The Klotho–insulin-like growth factor one axis has been discussed in relation to resilience, cognition, oxidative stress responses, and neurodegenerative vulnerability, all of which may overlap with depressive symptomatology. Although the annotation is not a direct statement about mood regulation, an anti-aging hormonal pathway that modulates insulin-like growth factor one signaling could plausibly influence depression risk through effects on neuroplasticity, energy homeostasis, inflammation, and stress biology. Therefore, FGF23 is noteworthy as a systemic regulator that may connect depression to broader aging- and metabolism-related disease mechanisms.  

Extending this growth factor-related theme, IGFBP4 is relevant to depression because insulin-like growth factor signaling has important roles in neurodevelopment, neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and stress adaptation. Disturbances in insulin-like growth factor signaling have been linked to mood disorders, cognitive impairment, and altered neurotrophic support. By controlling insulin-like growth factor bioavailability and receptor engagement, IGFBP4 may indirectly influence neuroplastic processes that are central to depression models, particularly those involving impaired trophic signaling and reduced capacity for adaptive remodeling in corticolimbic circuits. In addition, because insulin-like growth factor pathways intersect with inflammation and metabolic health, IGFBP4 may sit at the interface of endocrine and neurobiological mechanisms relevant to depressive illness. While the annotation is general, the regulatory position of IGFBP4 within the insulin-like growth factor axis makes it a meaningful candidate for depression-related interpretation.  

A further transition from growth factor regulation to broader signaling control highlights FSTL3, which is notable because it regulates activin and bone morphogenetic protein signaling, two branches of the transforming growth factor beta superfamily that have recognized relevance to neurodevelopment, synaptic plasticity, stress responses, and inflammatory regulation. Activin signaling in particular has been implicated in neuronal adaptation and affective behavior, suggesting that proteins that antagonize activin could influence depression-related pathways. The hematopoietic and stromal adhesion functions of FSTL3 also raise the possibility of broader immunological consequences, which is important given the growing evidence that depression is associated with altered immune cell composition and inflammatory signaling. Although the supplied annotation emphasizes developmental and hematopoietic functions rather than direct neuropsychiatric actions, its position as a modulator of transforming growth factor beta family signaling makes FSTL3 a biologically interesting candidate for linking peripheral regulatory systems to mood-related mechanisms.  

Shifting from signaling ligands and binding proteins to extracellular protease regulation, CST3 is potentially relevant to depression because protease regulation is important for extracellular matrix turnover, inflammatory processing, and tissue homeostasis, including in the central nervous system. Cystatin C has been studied in neurological and vascular contexts, and these domains are increasingly recognized as intersecting with depressive disorders, especially in late-life depression and depression associated with neurodegeneration or cerebrovascular disease. Through regulation of cysteine protease activity, CST3 may influence neuroinflammatory balance, neuronal vulnerability, and structural remodeling. Although the annotation is broad and does not explicitly mention the brain, the protein’s role as a protease inhibitor makes it a plausible contributor to biological processes that shape depression susceptibility or progression, particularly where inflammation or neurodegenerative change is prominent.  

Compared with the preceding proteins, CKAP4 appears less directly linked to established depression-related mechanisms, although it may still warrant cautious consideration. CKAP4 is less directly linked to depression than the immune- and growth-factor-related proteins in this list, but it may still be of interest because it mediates antiproliferative signaling. Depression has been associated with impaired neuroplasticity and, in some models, reduced cellular resilience or altered proliferative capacity in specific neural and peripheral compartments. A receptor involved in transmitting antiproliferative signals could therefore be relevant in a broader conceptual sense, particularly if future evidence connects CKAP4 signaling to stress-induced cellular remodeling, neurogenesis-related pathways, or epithelial–immune communication. On the basis of the provided annotation alone, however, its connection to depression remains more speculative than that of LGALS1, FGF23, IGFBP4, or FSTL3.  

An even more tentative interpretation applies to SHISA5, for which the currently supplied functional context is comparatively limited. SHISA5 is difficult to prioritize strongly for depression on the basis of the supplied annotation alone, because the function provided is limited to a difference in calcium affinity between isoforms. Nevertheless, calcium signaling is fundamentally important for neuronal excitability, synaptic transmission, and activity-dependent plasticity, all of which are central to depression biology. If SHISA5 participates more broadly in calcium-dependent cellular stress or apoptotic pathways, it could have relevance to mood disorder mechanisms. However, compared with the other proteins listed, the present evidence is too limited to support a robust depression-focused interpretation, and it should therefore be considered a lower-confidence candidate pending additional functional context.[[193]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10744743) 

Finally, MSLN appears to have the weakest apparent connection to depression within the current set, and its relevance remains particularly speculative on the basis of the annotation provided. MSLN is the least obviously connected to depression among the proteins listed. Its annotated function relates to megakaryocyte colony formation, suggesting a role in hematopoietic regulation rather than a direct role in neurobiology or affective processes. A speculative connection could be made through platelet biology, since platelets and megakaryocyte lineage cells are relevant to serotonin storage and inflammatory signaling, both of which have been implicated in depression. However, the supplied annotation does not provide sufficient mechanistic depth to support a strong disease link. Accordingly, MSLN should be regarded as a peripheral and currently low-priority candidate in the context of depression.
